solutions.check: 28 entries verified against the grid (lengths, crossings, linked-clue mapping)

clue.text: Beg before the main French pain in the arse

blocks.note: to bum something is to cadge or beg it
the main is the sea, which in French is la mer

explanation.surface: A beggar loitering by the French seafront is making a nuisance of himself.
explanation.walkthrough: 'The main' is an old poetic word for the open sea.
explanation.definitionFit: A bummer is slang for an annoying or disappointing thing, the same idea as a pain in the backside.

clue.text: One who pulls out (shock) of April – toe curling

indicators.note: curling twists something out of its straight line, so the letters are bent into a new order

blocks.note: the letters to be rearranged

explanation.surface: Someone yanks out a clump of hair in April and their toes curl in pain.
explanation.walkthrough: A shock here is a mass of hair, which is what this device pulls out.
explanation.definitionFit: An epilator is an electric gadget that removes hair by plucking it from the roots.

clue.text: see 8ac
Wind up RBS (pointless, in a mess)!

indicators.note: pointless means without a compass point, so one of the bank's letters that is a direction is dropped
things in a mess are jumbled, so the letters are thrown out of order

blocks.note: taken as written
the bank's initials with the S, for south, removed

explanation.surface: A jibe that the Royal Bank of Scotland, aimless and chaotic, is a load of hot air.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Wind up' looks like one phrase, but only 'Wind' defines; RBS is the Royal Bank of Scotland, and S is the compass point south.
explanation.definitionFit: Wind in the sense of gas from the stomach is what comes up in a belch.

clue.text: Copes, suppressing the last of Merkel's fulsome pants

indicators.note: the last of a word is its final letter, so only the end of the chancellor's name is used
to suppress something is to hold it down inside, so one piece is held within another

blocks.note: to fare is to get along or cope
final letter of the name

explanation.surface: Someone manages to keep a lid on Angela Merkel's pompous rhetoric.
explanation.walkthrough: Pants here means trousers, and fulsome stretches to mean full or generous in cut.
explanation.definitionFit: Flares are trousers that widen generously below the knee, so they are pants with plenty of material.

clue.text: It makes for a bad atmosphere getting tart to do a Brenda out loud

definitions.text: It makes for a bad atmosphere

indicators.note: out loud means spoken, so the word is chosen for its sound rather than its spelling

blocks.note: tart and acid both describe a sour taste
Brenda is Private Eye's nickname for the Queen, and what a queen does is reign

explanation.surface: A sour-faced woman playing at being the Queen spoils the mood of the room.
explanation.walkthrough: Brenda is Private Eye's long-running nickname for Queen Elizabeth II. The definition puns on atmosphere as both mood and air.
explanation.definitionFit: Acid rain is precipitation polluted by sulphur and nitrogen gases in the air, literally a bad atmosphere.

clue.text: Cocky politician gets in nevertheless – debts follow

indicators.note: to get in is to enter, so one piece goes inside the word for nevertheless

blocks.note: but means nevertheless or however
Member of Parliament
IOUs are written promises to pay debts

explanation.surface: An arrogant politician wins the seat anyway, and then the debts pile up.
explanation.definitionFit: Bumptious means self-assertive and full of oneself, which is what cocky describes.

clue.text: (& 3dn.) Boycott is balls – tick off

indicators.note: off means gone bad or wrong, so these letters are spoilt into a new order

blocks.note: the letters to be rearranged

explanation.surface: Someone dismisses a boycott as nonsense and gives it a telling-off.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Tick off' reads as a phrase meaning scold, but 'off' alone is the signal and 'tick' joins the fodder.
explanation.definitionFit: To blacklist something is to shun it by putting it on a banned list, which is a boycott.

clue.text: Nick's "guest" set up Fox

blocks.note: the nick is prison, whose reluctant guest is a convict
to found is to establish or set up

explanation.surface: A policeman's dubious visitor arranges a stitch-up of someone called Fox.
explanation.walkthrough: The nick is British slang for prison (or police station); a con is a convict.
explanation.definitionFit: To fox someone is to baffle or confuse them, which is what confound means.

clue.text: Slipper involved in one time fetish?

indicators.note: being involved in something puts you inside it, so one piece sits within others

blocks.note: a means one
a mule is a backless slipper
T is the abbreviation for time

explanation.surface: A slipper turns up in what looks like a one-off episode of foot fetishism.
explanation.walkthrough: Fetish is used in its older sense of an object believed to have magical power.
explanation.definitionFit: An amulet is a charm worn to ward off evil, an object credited with protective power like a fetish.

clue.text: Stick out belly embracing Rex Short

indicators.note: embracing means holding in one's arms, so one piece wraps around the abbreviation for king

blocks.note: a pot is a paunch or belly
R is the abbreviation for rex, Latin for king
short and rude both mean curt

explanation.surface: A paunch wrapping around a short man called Rex sticks out.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Short' looks like a description of Rex, but it is its own piece meaning curt.
explanation.definitionFit: To protrude is to project outward beyond a surface, which is to stick out.

clue.text: Backstabber Bush's opening routine against his nation

indicators.note: an opening is a start, so only the first letter of the president's name is used

blocks.note: first letter of the name
a rut is a dull routine
Bush's nation is the United States

explanation.surface: A traitor's view of George Bush's routine opening speech attacking his own country.
explanation.definitionFit: Brutus was among the assassins who stabbed Julius Caesar, his friend, making him the archetypal betrayer.

clue.text: Copper's having tantrum is more than healthy

blocks.note: a super is a police superintendent
a fit of temper is a tantrum

explanation.surface: A police officer throwing a tantrum is apparently in excellent health.
explanation.definitionFit: Superfit means extremely fit, beyond ordinary good health.

clue.text: Erection lost on TV series? Here's flannel

blocks.note: without an erection one is soft
a soap opera is a long-running TV serial

explanation.surface: A TV drama about losing an erection, sold to viewers with smooth talk.
explanation.walkthrough: Flannel is British slang for evasive or flattering talk, and also a washcloth, which sits nicely beside soap.
explanation.definitionFit: Soft soap is persuasive flattery, the same smooth evasive talk as flannel.

clue.text: (& 22dn.) Leader of Pakistan, beset by caste unrest, protecting Indian state's victim

indicators.note: the leader of a word is the letter at its front, so only the country's initial is used
unrest is disturbance, so the letters of the social class word are stirred up
something beset by others is surrounded by them, so the initial goes inside
protecting means shielding all round, so the state's name is held inside too

blocks.note: the letters of the word rearranged
first letter of the country
Goa is a state on India's west coast

explanation.surface: A Pakistani leader caught up in caste conflict shields a victim from an Indian state.
explanation.definitionFit: A scapegoat is someone made to bear the blame for others, a victim of misplaced punishment.

clue.text: Given Cameron's stand-off attitude to it, not much in evidence of late?

definitions.text: Given Cameron's stand-off attitude to it, not much in evidence of late?

blocks.clueFragment: Given Cameron's stand-off attitude to it
blocks.note: surface: a political body that David Cameron keeps at arm's length

blocks.clueFragment: not much in evidence of late
blocks.note: setter's reading: a pun on the name, since recently there has been little unity among its members

explanation.surface: Something David Cameron is aloof towards has hardly been seen lately.
explanation.walkthrough: David Cameron, as Prime Minister, took a semi-detached line on Brussels; the joke is that the organisation's own name promises a union that is barely visible.
explanation.definitionFit: The bloc of member states Britain belonged to, whose second word ironically claims a togetherness that was then lacking.

clue.text: Divorced party with Hello! piece, a major item of evidence in court

definitions.text: a major item of evidence in court

blocks.note: a former spouse is an ex
a greeting
a bit is a piece
taken as written

explanation.surface: A divorcee's interview in Hello! magazine becomes key evidence at trial.
explanation.walkthrough: Hello! is a British celebrity magazine, here simply a greeting.
explanation.definitionFit: Exhibit A is the first labelled item of evidence produced in a trial, and by extension the prime proof.

clue.text: Quality found in few politicians now cultivating dailies (Murdoch chiefly)?

definitions.text: Quality found in few politicians now

indicators.note: chiefly means at the head, so only the initial of the press baron is taken
cultivating turns over and works the soil, so the letters are worked into a new order

blocks.note: the letters of the word
first letter of the name

explanation.surface: Politicians who court Rupert Murdoch's newspapers have little principle left.
explanation.walkthrough: The joke is that sucking up to the Murdoch papers is exactly what kills principle in politicians.
explanation.definitionFit: Idealism is the pursuit of high principles over expediency, a virtue the setter finds rare in current politics.

clue.text: There's kinky: hugging copper's bloody cycle

indicators.note: kinky means twisted, so the letters of the opening words are bent out of order
hugging wraps around something, so these letters enclose the chemical symbol

blocks.note: the letters rearranged
Cu is the chemical symbol for copper

explanation.surface: A kinky scene of someone embracing a police officer during their bloody bike ride.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Copper' suggests a policeman, but it is the metal; 'cycle' suggests a bike but means the monthly one.
explanation.definitionFit: The curse is an old euphemism for menstruation, the monthly cycle involving bleeding.

clue.text: Isolated Blair, half gone, seen in clip

indicators.note: with half gone only the first half of the former prime minister's first name is kept
seen in means appearing inside, so the shortened name goes within the word for clip

blocks.note: a cuff is a clip round the ear
Tony Blair's first name with its second half removed

explanation.surface: Tony Blair, half out of the picture, shows up in a news clip looking isolated.
explanation.walkthrough: A clip and a cuff are both a light blow to the head.
explanation.definitionFit: Cut off means separated from others or unreachable, which is to be isolated.

clue.text: Rather sad, arse-grabbing Nixon, say, is completely gutted

indicators.note: a gutted word loses all its insides, so only its outer letters stay
grabbing means seizing and holding, so the outer letters clasp the word for bottom

blocks.note: Tricky Dicky was Richard Nixon's nickname, so a Dicky is an example of Nixon
the rear is the backside

explanation.surface: A grim image of President Nixon groping a backside, and being utterly devastated.
explanation.walkthrough: Gutted is also British slang for very disappointed, which makes the surface read like an emotional state.
explanation.definitionFit: Dreary means dull and gloomy, which is close to rather sad.

clue.text: Decline when Brenda backed Brown

indicators.note: backed means moved backwards, so the royal cipher is read from its end

blocks.note: Brenda is Private Eye's name for the Queen, whose cipher is ER
buff is a pale yellowish-brown colour

explanation.surface: The Queen turned down an invitation when she backed Gordon Brown.
explanation.walkthrough: ER, Elizabeth Regina, is the Queen's royal cipher; 'Brown' looks like Gordon Brown but is the colour.
explanation.definitionFit: To rebuff an offer is to refuse it bluntly, which is to decline it.

clue.text: Backing a git – bent bastard

indicators.note: bastard as an adjective means corrupted or impure, so the letters lose their original form

blocks.note: the letters to be rearranged

explanation.surface: Someone supports a scoundrel who is crooked through and through.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Bent' looks like the signal, since it means crooked, but it is fodder; the signal is 'bastard'.
explanation.definitionFit: Abetting means helping or encouraging someone, especially in wrongdoing, which is backing them.

clue.text: see 14dn.
The well known cold Lee's crushed and emptied balls

indicators.note: crushed things are squashed out of shape, so the name's letters are reordered
an emptied word has lost its contents, so only its first and last letters remain

blocks.note: C is the abbreviation for cold, as on a tap
the letters of the name rearranged
outer letters of the word

explanation.surface: A cold, crushed Lee is left drained, a painful image of an injury below the belt.
explanation.definitionFit: Celebs, short for celebrities, are famous people, so they are the well known.

clue.text: Pound Clegg's head to get on

indicators.note: the head of a name is its first letter, so only the Liberal Democrat's initial is used

blocks.note: first letter of the name
to get on is to grow older, to age

explanation.surface: An invitation to hit Nick Clegg over the head to make progress.
explanation.walkthrough: Nick Clegg was Liberal Democrat leader and deputy Prime Minister; 'Pound' looks like a verb, but it is the noun for an enclosure.
explanation.definitionFit: A pound is an enclosure for stray animals, so it is a kind of cage.

clue.text: Roger's pad

blocks.note: first meaning: vulgar slang for having sex with someone
second meaning: to fill or pad out a cushion

explanation.walkthrough: Roger looks like a man's name owning a flat; it is British slang for having sex, and pad is the verb to fill.
explanation.definitionFit: The word means both to have sex with, in crude slang, and to fill something with padding.

clue.text: Revolting, foul shag female makes light of

indicators.note: revolting also means rising in revolt, overturning order, so the letters are overturned

blocks.note: the letters to be rearranged
F is the abbreviation for female

explanation.surface: A woman shrugs off a disgusting, sordid sexual encounter.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Revolting' reads as disgusting, matching the surface, but it signals the rearrangement.
explanation.definitionFit: To laugh something off is to dismiss it with a joke, which is making light of it.
